chapters.title: Django REST Framework
chapters.subtitle: Serializers, viewsets, permissions and pagination
chapters.summary: DRF is the standard toolkit for Django APIs. The core is small: serializers convert objects to JSON and back, viewsets group CRUD actions, routers generate URLs, and permissions guard each action.
chapters.quick_answer: Install `djangorestframework`, add it to `INSTALLED_APPS`, define a `ModelSerializer` with explicit fields, expose it through a `ModelViewSet` and a router, and scope `get_queryset()` to the authenticated user. Never rely on the client to send only its own rows.

sections.title: Install and wire
sections.body:
DRF is a normal Django app. Add it to `INSTALLED_APPS`, include router URLs under `/api/`, and configure authentication and permissions globally or per view.

A global default of `IsAuthenticated` is safer than an open API with a few protected endpoints. Public endpoints should opt out explicitly.

sections.title: Serializers are the contract
sections.body:
A serializer defines which fields enter and leave the API. `ModelSerializer` infers fields from the model, but you should list them explicitly. `read_only_fields` protects server-controlled values; `extra_kwargs` sets validation.

Validation belongs in the serializer for API input. Do not let a client set `owner`, `tenant`, `is_staff` or `created_at` just because the model has those columns.

sections.title: ViewSets and routers
sections.body:
A `ModelViewSet` gives list, create, retrieve, update, partial update and destroy. A router generates the URL patterns. Override `get_queryset()` to scope data; override `perform_create()` to set fields the client must not control.

Use `APIView` or generic API views when the endpoint is not a simple CRUD shape. A viewset is a convenience, not a requirement.
sections.code:
from rest_framework import viewsets
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from .models import Post
from .serializers import PostSerializer

class PostViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = PostSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return (
            Post.objects.filter(author=self.request.user)
            .select_related("author")
            .order_by("-created_at")
        )

    def perform_create(self, serializer):
        serializer.save(author=self.request.user)

# urls.py
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter
from .views import PostViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("posts", PostViewSet, basename="post")
urlpatterns = router.urls

sections.title: Permissions and scoping
sections.body:
Authentication identifies the caller; permission classes decide whether the call is allowed; `get_queryset()` decides which rows exist for that caller. You need all three.

A common leak is a correct `IsAuthenticated` permission with an unscoped queryset, letting one user read another user's rows. Add a test that proves user B gets a 404 for user A's object.
sections.note: Object permissions run after `get_object()`. If the queryset is unscoped, the object can still be fetched before the permission check.

sections.title: Pagination, filtering and versioning
sections.body:
Paginate lists from day one; an unbounded list is a denial-of-service waiting for traffic. DRF's page-number pagination is fine for admin-style lists; cursor pagination is better for feeds and large tables because it does not drift when rows are inserted.

Add filtering explicitly with `django-filter` or a small `get_queryset()` parser. Version the API in the URL from the start (`/api/v1/`) so a breaking change does not break every client at once.

pitfalls: Using `fields = "__all__"` and letting clients write server-controlled fields.
An authenticated viewset with an unscoped queryset.
Returning an unpaginated list of every row.
Putting business logic in the serializer's `create()` instead of a service.
Changing a response shape without versioning the API.
checklist: Authentication and permission defaults are explicit.
Serializers list fields and mark server-controlled ones read-only.

chapters.title: Deployment
chapters.subtitle: From runserver to a boring, observable release
chapters.summary: A production Django deployment is mostly configuration: a real server, a real database, static files, migrations, secrets, health checks and logs. The framework is the easy part.
chapters.quick_answer: Run Django behind Gunicorn or Uvicorn, set `DEBUG=False`, use a production database, run `migrate` and `collectstatic` in the release, serve static files through WhiteNoise or a CDN, and add health checks and error tracking. Never expose `runserver`.

sections.title: The release artifact
sections.body:
Pin dependencies in `requirements.txt` or a lockfile. Build one artifact (container image or virtualenv) and promote the same artifact through staging and production. Do not build separately on each host; drift is how “works on staging” happens.

The release command should be idempotent: install, migrate, collect static, check, restart. If it fails halfway, re-running it should be safe.
sections.code:
# Dockerfile sketch
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
CMD ["gunicorn", "config.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3", "--timeout", "30"]

sections.title: WSGI or ASGI
sections.body:
`wsgi.py` is the synchronous entry point; Gunicorn is the common server. `asgi.py` supports async views and WebSockets; Uvicorn or Daphne is the server. Most CRUD sites are fine with WSGI.

Workers are processes. Start with `2 × CPU + 1` as a rough Gunicorn default, then measure. More workers increase memory and database connections; fewer workers queue requests. Set a request timeout so a stuck request does not hold a worker forever.

sections.title: Static files and the database
sections.body:
Run `collectstatic` during the build or release, then serve `STATIC_ROOT` with WhiteNoise (simple) or Nginx/CDN (faster). User media belongs in object storage, not on the app server's disk.

Use a managed PostgreSQL for multi-user production. Set `CONN_MAX_AGE` for persistent connections, but keep the total below the database's connection limit across all workers. Run migrations as a separate release step, not from every web worker at boot.

sections.title: Health checks and logs
sections.body:
A load balancer needs a cheap endpoint that proves the process is alive. A deeper check can prove the database is reachable, but do not make it expensive or expose internals publicly.

Send logs to stdout in production and let the platform collect them. Log request IDs, status codes, durations and exceptions. Add error tracking (Sentry or similar) with `DEBUG=False`; otherwise a 500 is invisible until a user reports it.

sections.title: The launch checklist
sections.body:
Before the first real user:

- `DEBUG=False` and a real `SECRET_KEY`.
- `ALLOWED_HOSTS` lists the exact hostnames.
- HTTPS redirect, secure cookies and HSTS are on.
- `migrate` and `collectstatic` run in the release.
- Static files are served by WhiteNoise, Nginx or a CDN.
- Uploads use object storage or a shared volume.
- Health and readiness endpoints exist.
- Logs and error tracking are connected.
- Database backups are scheduled and restored at least once in a drill.
- `python manage.py check --deploy` passes.

pitfalls: Running `migrate` from every web worker at boot and racing other workers.
Serving static files with Django instead of WhiteNoise or a web server.
Using SQLite for a multi-user production site.
Storing uploads on local disk behind a load balancer.
Having no health check, so a dead process keeps receiving traffic.
Skipping backups until the day the database is lost.
checklist: Migrations run once, before new workers take traffic.
Static files are collected and served efficiently.
Health, readiness, logs and error tracking are live.
A restore from backup has been tested.
